title: SYSK Selects: What Makes a One-hit Wonder?
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of a 2019 episode on the one-hit wonder phenomenon. The hosts trace the origin of the phrase (first seen in print in a July 1977 description of ABBA), discuss the Billboard Top 40 definition versus the looser cultural meaning, and run through one-hit wonders across the fifties, sixties, seventies, eighties and nineties in music, plus examples from sports (Eddie Gaedel, Chris Jelic), art (Harvey Ball's smiley face, Grant Wood), and literature (Harper Lee, J.D. Salinger, John Kennedy Toole, Sylvia Plath, Joseph Heller). They also discuss film directors (Michael Cimino, Steve Gordon's Arthur and its remake). The episode closes with listener mail from a listener whose wife doubts the show, and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and episode setup
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the Selects episode, and the hosts banter about the topic. They note there is little scholarly research on one-hit wonders, only lists, and discuss the psychology of being a one-hit wonder as a possible documentary topic.

segments.title: Origin of the phrase and the Billboard definition
segments.summary: The phrase's origin is unknown, but phrases.org cites a July 1977 print use describing ABBA. The conventional definition requires a Billboard Top 40 hit, and the hosts note how blurry that gets.

segments.title: Cultural one-hit wonders outside the Top 40
segments.summary: Legendary artists with one hit are discussed, including Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, Garth Brooks as Chris Gaines, and Beck. The hosts argue a one-hit wonder can be a song that captured a moment, such as Wallaby's Mexican Radio, even without a Top 40 placement.

segments.title: One-hit wonders by decade: fifties to seventies
segments.summary: The hosts list one-hit wonders from the fifties (Penguins' Earth Angel), sixties (Blue Cheer's Summertime Blues, Lemon Pipers' Green Tambourine), and seventies (Norman Greenbaum's Spirit in the Sky, Brewer and Shipley, Terry Jacks' Seasons in the Sun). They note disco's producer-driven one-hit wonders, and that Lips Inc. and Pseudo Echo both had hits with Funky Town.

segments.title: Eighties and nineties one-hit wonders abroad
segments.summary: The hosts discuss eighties one-hit wonders such as Soft Cell, Tony Basil, Bow Wow Wow, and Kajagoogoo. They note that a-ha had Take On Me in the US and a later top-twenty hit, and that Right Said Fred, Frankie Goes to Hollywood, Gary Numan, and Falco were bigger abroad. They also mention Crash Test Dummies and Faith No More's Epic in the nineties.

segments.title: One-hit wonders in sports
segments.summary: The hosts describe one-hit wonders in baseball, noting players with one hit that was a home run. They discuss Eddie Gaedel, a little person who drew four walks in a 1951 Yankees game and whose jersey is in the Hall of Fame.

segments.title: Art world one-hit wonders
segments.summary: Harvey Ball, who created the 1971 smiley face for a State Mutual Life Assurance morale campaign and was paid $240, never had another artistic hit. Grant Wood, painter of American Gothic, became a celebrity and withdrew from the spotlight, and the hosts discuss seeing famous artworks in person.

segments.title: Literary and film one-hit wonders
segments.summary: Harper Lee (To Kill a Mockingbird), J.D. Salinger (The Catcher in the Rye), and John Kennedy Toole (A Confederacy of Dunces, published after his suicide) are discussed, along with Sylvia Plath (The Bell Jar) and Joseph Heller (Catch-22). Michael Cimino's Heaven's Gate is described as a notorious failure. Steve Gordon's Arthur and its remake are discussed.

segments.title: Sponsor read
segments.summary: A sponsor break promoting the show's sponsor.

segments.title: Listener mail: Devin and his wife Elizabeth
segments.summary: A listener named Devin says his wife Elizabeth thinks the show is stoner banter, and asks for a shout-out to her. The hosts respond that the show is not written under the influence, and tell him to let Elizabeth listen.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close with social media and website information and the show's production credits.
